name: Rhino 3D
tagline: General purpose NURBS surface modeler used heavily in jewelry, product design and architecture.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Sold as a one-time perpetual license with paid version upgrades, so a monthly figure does not apply.

verdictSummary: The thing you would be rebuilding is not an app, it is a NURBS geometry kernel with thirty years of edge case handling in it: trimmed surfaces, fillets that do not explode, booleans that survive being sent to a caster. An agent can absolutely give you a parametric ring or pendant generator in an afternoon, and that is genuinely useful if your work is a family of similar shapes with changing dimensions. It cannot give you free-form surface modeling, watertight solids you would trust a $400 platinum print on, Grasshopper, or STEP and 3DM interoperability with the bench and the printing service. Jewelry also has an ecosystem layer: RhinoGold, Matrix, Panther, Clayoo, plus every tutorial and hired contractor assuming you are in Rhino. A weekend build replaces a configurator, not a modeler.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that generates parametric ring bands, signet faces and simple bezel settings from numeric inputs and exports a printable STL.
requirements: Willingness to check wall thickness and shrinkage yourself
A print or casting service that accepts STL
Ring size chart for diameter mapping
whatYouLose: Free-form surface modeling: anything organic, sculpted or not expressible as parameters is off the table
A trustworthy solid modeling kernel: mesh booleans leave non-manifold edges that printers and casters reject
Grasshopper and the jewelry plugin ecosystem, including gem libraries, prong generators and hallmark tooling
File interoperability, 3DM, STEP, IGES, so nobody downstream can open or edit your geometry
Drafting, dimensioning, rendering and the fifteen quiet tools you did not know you used until they were gone
moatNotes: The real asset is the geometry kernel and its tolerance behavior, which is exactly the kind of code that takes decades and cannot be vibed.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a one-time license is cheap relative to one botched cast, and because Rhino sits at the center of a supply chain. The casting house, the CNC shop, the 3D printing bureau and the freelancer you hire all speak 3DM and STEP. Even jewelers who only ever build variations on the same eight designs keep paying, since the moment a client asks for something asymmetric or hand sculpted, a parametric configurator is a dead end and Rhino is not.
notes: A ring configurator is a weekend; a NURBS modeler is not. The moat is a thirty year old geometry kernel plus every caster, printer and contractor downstream expecting its file formats.
prompt:
Build a local, offline parametric jewelry generator that runs in the browser. This is a consolation build for people who only need dimensional variations of a few known shapes, not a CAD replacement.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + TypeScript, three.js for viewport and geometry, three-bvh-csg for booleans, lil-gui for the parameter panel. No backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no analytics. Everything runs from a static build.

In scope:
1. A viewport with orbit controls, a shaded material, a soft studio-ish three light setup and a 10mm reference grid.
2. Three generators, each a pure function from a params object to a THREE.BufferGeometry:
   - Band: ring size (US 3 to 13, mapped to inner diameter via a table you hardcode), width, thickness, profile (flat, half round, knife edge), optional comfort fit inner dome, optional taper toward the back.
   - Signet: a band plus a top face, face shape (oval, cushion, round), face length, width, dome height, boolean unioned to the band.
   - Bezel: a band plus a cylindrical or oval bezel cup with wall thickness, seat ledge and a through hole under the stone, boolean subtracted.
3. Live parameter panel with numeric inputs in millimeters. Regenerate on change, debounced.
4. A measurement readout: bounding box, estimated volume in cubic mm, and estimated cast weight for silver, 14k gold and platinum using hardcoded densities.
5. A manufacturability check that runs after each build: report minimum wall thickness found by sampling, flag anything under 0.8mm, and run a manifold check (every edge used exactly twice) with a loud red warning if it fails.
6. Export binary STL and OBJ to disk via a download. Also export the params object as JSON, and support re-importing that JSON.
7. A presets list stored in localStorage so a design is one click away next time.

Out of scope, do not attempt: free-form surface editing, NURBS, fillet tools, text engraving, gem libraries, rendering, anything cloud.

Use tessellation resolution as a top level setting, default coarse for interaction and re-run at fine before export. Write a README that states plainly what this cannot do and tells the user to verify wall thickness with their caster before spending money on metal.
